title: Scholarships for Public Schools
author: Josh Cowen
summary: Josh Cowen, a Michigan State education policy professor and long-time critic of school vouchers, argues in a guest post for Alexander Russo's The Grade that the new federal scholarship tax credit (FSTC) differs from earlier voucher schemes in ways that matter to public schools. State voucher budgets suffer because most users were never in public school, but the FSTC is open to public school students who stay put and can be a revenue source for districts, funding tutoring, afterschool enrichment and summer school. Treasury projects it could reach at least $26 billion by 2030. Because governors must opt in each year and donors can give to any state, Cowen expects most states to join within two years. The remaining obstacle is that Democratic governors distrust the Trump administration, and he does not blame them for caution.
points: Cowen says his voucher critiques remain empirical and still apply to many features of the new federal credit.
Unlike state vouchers, the FSTC lets public school students remain enrolled and lets districts receive funds for enrichment and tutoring.
Treasury indicates the credit could be worth at least $26 billion by 2030.
The opt-in design puts pressure on governors, since donations will simply flow to participating states, so he predicts most will join.
Democratic governors' distrust of the Trump administration is the main reason some blue states may hold back for now.
quotes: My criticism of school vouchers has always been empirical, first and foremost.
The fact that the vast majority of voucher users were never in public schools translates into a new state expenditure — not a cost savings.

for the first time ever — to my knowledge — a voucher-like program is available to public school students who remain in their public schools — and is available as a revenue source for public school districts.
the U.S. Treasury indicates the FSTC could be worth at least $26 billion by 2030.
The so-called “opt-in” requirement in the FSTC — governors must elect their states to participate each year — creates a bind for governors who stay out.
I believe it does school leaders, educators, and parents a disservice to deny the existence of that money.
Conservative education reformers are essentially asking Democrats to take a leap of faith on a policy that will require some creativity and some new organization to leverage.
